original_question: Fix r > 0. A maximal distance minimizer (also called an r-minimizer) for a compact set M \subset \mathbb{R}^d is a connected compact set \Sigma of minimal length (one-dimensional Hausdorff measure H^1(\Sigma)) among connected compact sets satisfying M \subset B_r(\Sigma), where B_r(\Sigma) is the closed r-neighborhood of \Sigma. Let M be an R-stadium, defined as the boundary of the R-neighborhood of a segment. For parameters satisfying r < R < 5r, describe the set of maximal distance minimizers for this R-stadium. Additionally, determine (i) the supremum of constants C such that there exists a maximal distance minimizer for a Cr-neighborhood that is not a horseshoe, and (ii) the infimum of constants c such that for any closed curve with minimal radius of curvature cr, every maximal distance minimizer is a horseshoe.
target_in_paper: Section 1.1, Question 1.2: the planar R-stadium classification problem, together with the two threshold subquestions stated immediately below it. This is the closest official formulation to your draft. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.18217v1))
correct_elements: The draft already captures the correct variational definition of an r-minimizer/maximal distance minimizer, the stadium input, the open regime r<R<5r, and the fact that the paper breaks the stadium problem into two sharp-threshold subquestions about when non-horseshoe minimizers can occur and when horseshoes are forced. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.18217v1))
missing_details: The paper’s stadium question is planar: the relevant ambient space is R^2, since an R-stadium is the boundary of the R-neighborhood of a line segment in the plane. Your opening definition in R^d is fine as background, but the research question itself should be specialized to R^2. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.18217v1))

The phrase “a maximal distance minimizer for a Cr-neighborhood” is ambiguous. The paper’s intent is a Cr-stadium, i.e. the boundary of the closed Cr-neighborhood of a segment, not an arbitrary neighborhood. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.18217v1))

The term “horseshoe” should be defined inside the question. In the nearby context, it means an arc of the inner/parallel curve together with two tangent segments at the endpoints of that arc. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.18217v1))

For the second threshold constant, the nearby theorem context is about closed convex curves with minimal radius of curvature at least c r; your draft omits the convexity hypothesis and the ‘at least’ quantifier. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.18217v1))

The paper also records a useful stadium-specific structural reduction: minimizers for an R-stadium are built from line segments and curves parallel to the stadium’s circular arcs. That is not essential to state the problem, but it is part of the paper-faithful scope. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.18217v1))
refined_question: In the planar maximal-distance-minimizer problem, fix r>0 and let M⊂R^2 be an R-stadium, meaning the boundary of the closed R-neighborhood of a line segment. Determine the set of all r-minimizers Σ for M in the open regime r<R<5r. More sharply, determine the sharp constant C_*:=sup{C>0: for some Cr-stadium there exists an r-minimizer that is not a horseshoe} and the sharp constant c_*:=inf{c>0: for every closed convex curve M with minimal radius of curvature at least c r, every r-minimizer for M is a horseshoe}, where a horseshoe is the union of an arc of the inner parallel curve of M at distance r and two tangent segments at the endpoints of that arc. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.18217v1))
justification: Your draft is clearly aimed at Question 1.2 in §1.1 rather than the neighboring circle problem, because it asks about R-stadiums, uses the same open window r<R<5r, and includes exactly the two threshold-constant directions the paper appends immediately below the stadium question. I kept your formulation narrow and paper-faithful, while sharpening the hidden assumptions that the paper leaves implicit in nearby context: the planar setting, the meaning of “horseshoe,” the fact that the first constant concerns Cr-stadiums, and the curvature-threshold formulation for closed convex curves. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/html/2511.18217v1))
